html:
A long running scheme to move landless families from crowded Java, and to a lesser extent Bali, Lombok and Madura, to the less populated outer islands of Indonesia. The Dutch began it in 1905 and independent Indonesia expanded it greatly.

Under the colonial Ethical Policy, Dutch officials worried about poverty on Java and sent the first settlers to Lampung in south Sumatra in 1905. After independence the programme became a symbol of national unity. It peaked under Suharto in the late 1970s and 1980s, with help from the World Bank. Millions of people were moved to Sumatra, Kalimantan, Sulawesi, Maluku and Papua, each family given a plot of land, a house and help for the first years.

The results were mixed. Some settlements prospered, while others failed on poor soils. Large areas of forest were cleared. Local peoples often lost land, and critics in Papua saw it as a way to swamp them with outsiders. Tensions between newcomers and local people fed later violence, as in the Sampit conflict in Kalimantan in 2001. See Dutch East Indies and Indonesia.
